name: Rapamycin
lead: Rapamycin, also called sirolimus and sold under the brand name Rapamune among others, is a macrolide compound produced by the soil bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus. It was first isolated in the early 1970s from a soil sample taken on Easter Island (Rapa Nui), which gave the compound its name.[1] It was first studied as an antifungal, but its potent immunosuppressive and antiproliferative properties, which arise from inhibiting the kinase mTOR, redirected its development.[1][2]

It is a prescription drug used to prevent organ transplant rejection (particularly in kidney transplantation), to treat the rare lung disease lymphangioleiomyomatosis, to coat coronary stents, and, in a protein-bound form, to treat a rare tumour called PEComa. It is also used in vascular malformations and, topically, for facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis complex.[1] Because inhibiting mTOR extends lifespan in several animal species, rapamycin has become the most discussed prescription drug in longevity communities, where some people use it off-label.[3][15]

Evidence for human anti-aging benefit remains preliminary. A 2024 Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review of 19 studies found improvements in some physiological parameters of ageing in immune, cardiovascular and skin systems, no significant effects on endocrine, muscular or neurological systems, and increased infections and raised cholesterol and triglycerides in people with age-related diseases.[3] A small exploratory trial of topical rapamycin reported reduced skin senescence markers,[5] but no trial has shown that rapamycin changes visible appearance or extends human lifespan.

paras: In the United States sirolimus (Rapamune) is indicated to prevent rejection in renal transplant recipients aged 13 and older and to treat lymphangioleiomyomatosis, with the latter approval in May 2015 making it the first drug approved for that disease. A protein-bound formulation (Fyarro) is approved for advanced PEComa.[1][6] Its chief advantage over calcineurin inhibitors in transplantation is lower kidney toxicity.[1] In the EU, topical sirolimus (Hyftor) is approved for facial angiofibroma associated with tuberous sclerosis complex.[1]

Sirolimus-eluting coronary stents reduce restenosis compared with bare-metal stents, and sirolimus-coated balloons are being compared with paclitaxel-coated balloons.[1][7][8] Sirolimus is also used in vascular anomalies and has been studied in children with slow-flow vascular malformations in a randomised trial,[9] as well as in tuberous sclerosis complex[10] and epilepsy linked to focal cortical dysplasia.[11] Analogues such as temsirolimus are used in cancers such as renal cell carcinoma.[12]

The case for rapamycin in ageing rests on animal research showing lifespan extension and on the central role of mTOR in nutrient sensing, growth and autophagy.[13][14] Reviews describe mTOR as a regulator of ageing processes.[3][15] Some people take low-dose, intermittent off-label rapamycin under physician supervision. Some commentary in the community frames this as an attempt to slow ageing, including skin ageing, although no study has tested systemic rapamycin for appearance outcomes.

Topical use is a separate strand: a 2019 exploratory randomised trial in GeroScience tested topical rapamycin on human skin and examined markers of senescence and ageing.[5] A registered phase 2 trial is testing topical rapamycin for vitiligo.[16] Facial angiofibromas in tuberous sclerosis are a disfiguring condition for which topical sirolimus has shown positive results in reviewed reports, with improvement in a large majority of the 84 patients described in one review cited by Wikipedia.[1]

Sirolimus binds the cytosolic protein FKBP12, and that complex inhibits mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1), which is how it blocks T and B cell activation and signalling by interleukins such as IL-2.[1][17] This differs from tacrolimus, which forms a complex with the same binding protein but inhibits calcineurin.[1] The mTOR pathway integrates nutrient, growth-factor and energy signals to regulate growth, metabolism and autophagy, and has been implicated in cancer, diabetes and ageing.[4][13][14][18] Research has shown that AMPK and mTOR regulate autophagy through phosphorylation of Ulk1,[14] and that the rictor-containing mTOR complex phosphorylates Akt.[19] Longer exposure can also affect mTORC2, which Wikipedia links to diabetes-like effects such as reduced glucose tolerance; in mice such effects were avoided with alternative dosing regimens or analogues.[1]

Sirolimus is metabolised by CYP3A4 and is a substrate of the P-glycoprotein pump, so inhibitors of either may raise blood levels and inducers may lower them.[1] A registered study compared the bioavailability of compounded and generic rapamycin in people of normal ageing.[20]

The US label carries a boxed warning for immunosuppression, with increased susceptibility to infection and possible development of lymphoma and other malignancies, and states that use is not recommended in liver or lung transplant patients.[21] Warnings and precautions in the label include hypersensitivity reactions, angioedema, fluid accumulation, impaired wound healing, hyperlipidaemia, decline in renal function, proteinuria, latent viral infections and interstitial lung disease or non-infectious pneumonitis.[21] The label also states that sirolimus can cause fetal harm based on animal studies and its mechanism.[21]

In transplant trials the most common adverse reactions include peripheral oedema, raised cholesterol and triglycerides, hypertension, raised creatinine, anaemia and infections; in lymphangioleiomyomatosis, mouth and lip ulcers, acne and diarrhoea were commonly reported.[1] Pulmonary toxicity is a recognised complication, particularly in lung transplant recipients, and the mechanism is unclear.[1] Sirolimus-induced lymphoedema has been described in case reports.[22] Wikipedia notes warnings that sirolimus may raise mortality in some transplant settings through infection risk, increased risk of skin cancer and lymphoma, and delayed wound healing, especially in people with BMI above 30.[1]

Longevity-related human studies. The 2024 Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review identified 19 studies from 18,400 articles and reported improvements in physiological parameters of ageing in the immune, cardiovascular and integumentary systems, but no significant effects on endocrine, muscular or neurological systems. It reported no serious adverse events attributed to rapamycin or rapalogs in healthy individuals but more infections and increases in total and LDL cholesterol and triglycerides in people with age-related diseases, and noted that long-term exposure has not been tested.[3] The PEARL randomised trial reported safety and healthspan metrics after one year of rapamycin dosing in healthy adults in Aging in 2025.[23] The 2019 topical study was exploratory and prospective, with senescence markers as the main outcome.[5]

Established indications. Randomised trials support use in transplantation, including a large trial of reduced calcineurin-inhibitor exposure in renal transplantation involving 1,645 recipients,[24] and in LAM, where a placebo-controlled trial in 89 patients for 12 months informed approval.[1] Registered trials cover topical rapamycin for angiofibromas in TSC (n=179),[25] Peutz-Jeghers syndrome,[26] venous malformations,[27] and uterine fibroids.[28] Glucocorticoid-free islet transplantation regimens using sirolimus were reported in seven patients in 2000.[29] A 2026 trial examined sirolimus-coated balloons in infrainguinal artery disease.[8]
No studies were found testing oral rapamycin for visible skin, hair or facial appearance in healthy people.

Rapamycin was isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus in soil collected on Easter Island; Wikipedia gives 1972 as the first isolation, while Grokipedia describes a 1964 expedition and a 1975 report from Ayerst Laboratories, now part of Pfizer.[1][6][31] It was developed first as an antifungal with strong activity against Candida, then abandoned for that use once its immunosuppressive and antiproliferative properties were recognised.[1][31][30] The FDA approved it on 15 September 1999 for kidney transplant rejection prophylaxis.[6] Research on its target, TOR, began with yeast mutants resistant to the drug, and the protein was later named mammalian target of rapamycin.[1] Landmark mTOR reviews now rank among the most-cited in the field.[13][18]

Rapamycin is a prescription drug in the US, UK and EU, and use for ageing is off-label; community members describe obtaining it through physicians or compounding arrangements. On T Nation, forum members mention rapamycin alongside resveratrol and caloric restriction in discussions of life extension, with one 2010 post noting that direct TOR blocking is a heavy-handed approach because rapamycin strongly suppresses the immune system.[32][33] Many other T Nation threads mention mTOR only in the context of muscle protein synthesis and leucine, rather than the drug itself.[34][35] No looksmax.org or Reddit material was identified.

timeline.event: Rapamycin is isolated from Streptomyces hygroscopicus in an Easter Island soil sample, per Wikipedia.[1]
FDA approves sirolimus (Rapamune) for prophylaxis of kidney transplant rejection.[6]
Islet transplantation in seven type 1 diabetes patients with a glucocorticoid-free sirolimus regimen is reported.[29]
FDA approves sirolimus for lymphangioleiomyomatosis, the first drug approved for it.[1]
Exploratory trial of topical rapamycin on human skin senescence markers is published.[5]
Lancet Healthy Longevity systematic review of rapamycin and rapalogs in human ageing.[3]
PEARL trial reports one-year safety and healthspan metrics.[23]

lore.intro: In longevity circles rapamycin is treated as a leading candidate to slow ageing; community discussion on T Nation is sparse and often conflates the drug with the mTOR pathway.[32][33][34]

claims.claim: Rapamycin slows ageing because it inhibits mTOR
claims.believers: Proponents point to the pathway's role in ageing and to lifespan extension in animals, and describe the drug as the leading intervention targeting that pathway.[13][18]
claims.experts: A 2024 systematic review found improvements in some physiological ageing parameters but no effect on others, with higher infection and lipid levels in people with age-related disease, and called for studies of long-term exposure.[3]

claims.claim: Low-dose or intermittent rapamycin avoids the side effects seen in transplant patients
claims.believers: Off-label users argue that lower or intermittent exposure avoids the immunosuppression seen at transplant doses.[32]
claims.experts: The 2025 PEARL trial and the 2024 review reported no serious adverse events attributed to rapamycin in healthy individuals, but the label's boxed warnings relate to transplant dosing, and long-term safety in healthy people has not been established.[3][21][23]

claims.claim: Rapamycin is too blunt an instrument for healthy people
claims.believers: A 2010 T Nation poster says directly blocking TOR is too heavy a hammer because rapamycin is a powerful immune suppressant, favouring resveratrol instead.[33]
claims.experts: The label warns of infection, malignancy, impaired wound healing, hyperlipidaemia and pneumonitis in transplant populations, while healthy-adult data are limited.[21][3]

claims.believers: Interest follows from research linking mTOR to cellular senescence and from reports of topical use for facial angiofibromas.[5][1]
claims.experts: A small exploratory randomised trial reported effects on senescence markers in human skin; no trial has shown improved visible ageing in healthy people.[5]

claims.believers: Bodybuilding forum posts describe mTOR as the switch for muscle protein synthesis, triggered by leucine and mechanical tension, so blocking it is assumed to hinder gains.[34][35]
claims.experts: The 2024 review found no significant effect of rapamycin on the muscular system in human studies, but it did not assess strength training outcomes in detail.[3]
